title: Lifelong-learning systems face an institutionalization gap between policy ambition and everyday implementation
source_unit: International Labour Organization, Independent High-Level Evaluation of the ILO’s strategies and actions under the ILO strategy on skills and lifelong learning, 2022–2026, 2026
geography: Comparative evaluation covering six country case studies: Colombia, Panama, Kenya, Ethiopia, Republic of Moldova, and Bangladesh; broader ILO portfolio evidence

observations.period: 2022–2026; evaluation of the ILO Skills and Lifelong Learning 2030 strategy and action plan

strategic_relevance.value: the strategy remains highly relevant as a framework linking skills and lifelong learning to decent work, productive employment, social inclusion, and just transitions

strongest_contribution.value: the strongest contributions were in governance, evidence-informed policy, institutional capacity, qualifications systems, recognition of prior learning, quality apprenticeships, social dialogue, and skills-needs intelligence

institutionalization_gap.value: progress was more limited in operational implementation, routine use of intelligence, sustainable financing, and scaling reforms in national systems

mechanism.value: skills policy becomes durable when strategic frameworks are translated into funded institutions, implementation capacity, domestic ownership, and routine use beyond externally supported projects

observations.method: Independent high-level evaluation using ILO document review, six country case studies, interviews and surveys with staff, constituents, donors, UN and other partners, and synthesis of 95 relevant evaluation reports.
observations.uncertainty: The evaluation is a strategy-level assessment rather than a causal estimate of labor-market effects; country contexts and implementation readiness vary, and large-scale employment, productivity, and inclusion impacts remain difficult to attribute to ILO support.
observations.subgroup: Workers needing upskilling or reskilling, women, youth, migrants, refugees, persons with disabilities, informal-economy workers, employers, training providers, worker and employer organizations, and public skills authorities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Slow implementation may reflect weak labor demand, macroeconomic conditions, political discontinuity, or underfunding outside the ILO’s control rather than a failure of skills policy design alone.

observations.period: 2022–2026; distribution of participation and institutional voice in skills governance

tripartite_asymmetry.value: government led TVET and lifelong-learning activity; employers contributed to identifying skills priorities; workers’ organizations had formal governance roles but more limited influence

participation_mode.value: constituent participation was predominantly consultative rather than strategic and operational

lifelong_learning_shift.value: implementation remained concentrated on initial skills development and TVET reform, with comparatively less emphasis on upskilling and reskilling throughout working life

mechanism.value: the social legitimacy of lifelong learning depends on moving worker voice from consultation into the design, implementation, and accountability of transition systems

observations.method: Cross-case evaluation of ILO interventions, constituent interviews and surveys, portfolio review, and assessment against relevance and coherence criteria.
observations.uncertainty: The finding describes the ILO portfolio and reported stakeholder participation; it does not measure the full distribution of worker voice across national skills systems or establish which participation model produces better outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Workers in changing occupations, informal workers, women, youth, migrants, employers, worker organizations, training institutions, and governments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Employer-led priority setting can improve labor-market relevance, while worker organizations may face capacity or resource constraints; formal participation alone may not guarantee substantive influence.

observations.period: 2026; recommendations for the next implementation cycle through 2030

implementation_priority.value: the evaluation recommends measurable milestones, beneficiary and outcome tracking, systemic-leverage prioritization, institutional change management, sustainable financing, scale-up, and stronger tripartite engagement

programmatic_solution.value: the Global Skills Programme’s coordination, technical backstopping, common methods, peer learning, and system-oriented reform functions are recommended for institutionalization across regions

sustainability_condition.value: domestic financing, institutional capacity, national ownership, implementation incentives, and political continuity determine whether reforms survive beyond externally funded projects

mechanism.value: policy pilots become social infrastructure only when evidence, financing, institutional mandates, and adaptive learning are connected to a repeatable implementation system

observations.method: Evaluation synthesis of implementation, effectiveness, efficiency, impact orientation, sustainability, and recommendations for the 2026–2030 period.
observations.uncertainty: Recommendations are forward-looking institutional guidance, not evidence that the proposed reforms will produce specific employment, wage, or inclusion effects; financing and political continuity remain external risks.
observations.subgroup: National skills authorities, training providers, workers and employers, sector institutions, donors, development partners, and people navigating technological or environmental work transitions.
observations.counterinterpretation: More monitoring and institutional machinery can increase reporting burdens or centralize control; system-level coordination must preserve local adaptation and avoid reducing learning to employer-demand metrics.

boundary: This record identifies an institutionalization gap in lifelong-learning systems: policy and governance reforms are advancing faster than routine implementation, domestic financing, worker influence, and scale. It is an independent strategy-level evaluation, not causal proof that skills reforms improve wages, employment, productivity, or inclusion; the next test is whether national systems convert policy frameworks into durable, accessible, worker-legitimate learning and transition institutions.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ILO evaluation PDF and publication page, executive assessment, 95-report evidence base, six country cases, key findings on relevance, tripartite participation, lifelong-learning emphasis, implementation, financing, sustainability, and recommendations were reviewed.
